invalid_failure_risks: The exact manifest/checksum algorithm, SQLite derived-table replacement policy, and recovery precedence between existing catalog rows and segment history are not stated normatively; relying on inference from tools may make a correct implementation appear wrong.

The instruction requires writes to be atomic enough that a restart cannot expose partial state, but the described tests do not specify crash points, durability guarantees, or whether fsync-level atomicity is required.

The malformed-frame rule (terminate at the last safe boundary rather than skip to later bytes) and the precise total ordering are primarily in the internal hint, so a solver may have no reliable way to distinguish intended behavior from plausible alternatives.
Tests that compare raw SQLite row sets can overconstrain implementation details not exposed by the protocol unless the expected schema, ordering, and treatment of derived rows are fixed.
Verify-time fixture generation and shared writable state could be flaky if each scenario does not reset the catalog, segment directory, and process environment completely.

The under-one-hour solvability target is optimistic for reverse-engineering an undocumented binary format, repairing several persistence paths, and validating six generated histories on a one-CPU container.
review.reasons: The task has a coherent real-world failure mode, strong cross-component verification, and enough edge cases to defeat superficial fixes. Its intended behavior is mostly inferable from the supplied tools and fixtures, although several persistence and checksum semantics should be made more explicit; the scores still clear the acceptance threshold.
fixes: Add a concise normative recovery section to PROTOCOL.md defining transaction ordering, malformed-frame termination, catalog-versus-segment precedence, and idempotent replacement semantics.
Specify the manifest generation and digest algorithm, canonical serialization, and exactly which SQLite rows are authoritative versus derived.
Define the required durability boundary for put/delete and either add an injected-crash test or narrow the requirement to transactional restart consistency.
State the exact expected SQLite row-set normalization used by the verifier, including ordering and treatment of empty tenants and tombstones.
Make every scenario use an isolated copied state directory and document resource and timeout limits for generated fixtures.

verdicts.reason: Both involve deterministic replay into SQLite, but this task is a multi-tenant segment-based key/value recovery service with live protocol operations, whereas the reference is incident correlation, alias resolution, and state-transition migration.
Although both expose audit-related results, this task reconstructs key/value state and event history from damaged segments, not cryptographically verifies and filters signed audit chains.
This task repairs a stdin/stdout replay and persistence service, while the reference builds an HTTP metrics query service around a native aggregation engine.
Both require consistent replayed persistent state and idempotence, but the candidate concerns segment recovery and tenant key/value semantics rather than campaign funnel attribution and reporting.
The reference is a TCP HMAC serialization service for binary WAL records, whereas the candidate is a stateful segment replay, catalog repair, and JSON protocol service.
